newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong prepares to draft new election laws.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong prepares to draft new election laws.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government is preparing to draft new electoral laws that will undo at a stroke the reforms sponsored by Governor Chris Patten that infuriated China, Hong Kong newspapers said on Friday.

The China-appointed Preparatory Committee, a 150-member body established in December 1995 to steer Hong Kong through its transition to China, is drawing up a set of proposals to govern the first post-colonial elections.
Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, a date now 54 days away.
The Hong Kong Economic Journal said Hong Kong's future leader, former shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, had discussed the issue with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Beijing last week.

The Chinese-language Ming Pao quoted Preparatory Committee member and Hong Kong academic Lau Siu-kai, who chairs the panel studying the electoral changes, as saying the committee was expected to recommend a multiple-seat, single-vote system to replace the current first-past-the-post system.
The idea is to hammer out a broad framework to lay before Tung's post-1997 Hong Kong administration, which will be responsible for formulating the precise details, Lau said.
"It will give more room for Mr Tung and his executive councillors to decide the details, and draft an electoral bill for the Provisional Legislative Council before the handover," Lau told reporters.

Patten's democratic reforms, which governed the 1995 elections, widened the franchise and rid Hong Kong's legislative council of appointed members for the first time, but at the cost of angering China.
Beijing responded by pledging to dissolve the elected council when it resumed sovereignty of Hong Kong and replace it with an appointed provisional legislature.
Members of a provisional legislature -- including a number of pro-Beijing politicians defeated in the 1995 polls -- were selected last December and are expected to serve for about a year.

Hong Kong opinion polls indicate residents of the British colony are wary but generally neutral about the provisional legislature but want to see elections held as soon as possible after the handover.
But the planned interim provisional legislature has inflamed Hong Kong's democratic lobby, which has campaigned at home and abroad against the chamber that it describes as unconstitutional.
The populist Democratic Party, led by lawyer Martin Lee, has pledged to sue the provisional legislature if it seeks to pass legislation ahead of the handover.
The party boycotted the provisional legislature selection process and faces months in the political wilderness. It plans to contest the first post-handover elections in 1998.

Hong Kong's outgoing colonial government also refuses to recognise the provisional legislature and has witheld assistance for the body -- hampering its attempts to draft laws and amendments, Tung's aides said.
Tung's office has only two law drafters on its staff.
